Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- The often scathing critic Simon Cowell called Susan Boyle -- the breakout singing sensation from "Britain's Got Talent" -- a "little tiger." Judge Piers Morgan admits that he expected Susan Boyle's audition to be a joke before she began singing. On CNN's "Larry King Live," she showed she's no one-trick pony. During a taping of the show Friday, she nailed a verse of Celine Dion's "My Heart Will Go On" after King asked her to sing. "Amazing. That was just absolutely stunning," said "Britain's Got Talent" judge Piers Morgan, who was also a guest. "To sing that with no musical backing is unbelievable. You have the voice of an angel, Susan." The 47-year-old Boyle's frumpy attire and awkward mannerisms drew snickers and eye-rolling from her audience before she belted out a pitch-perfect number from "Les Miserables" at an audition for the talent contest, making her an overnight sensation.  Watch Boyle sing on Larry King » . An unemployed charity worker who lives alone with her cat in Scotland, Boyle has inspired millions with a performance that flies in the face of pop music's penchant for pre-processed princesses. A clip of her audition had more than 19 million views on YouTube by Friday evening. Boyle, who did a repeat performance of "I Dreamed a Dream" via satellite on CNN's "Anderson Cooper 360" Thursday night, told King she was aware of the snickers her appearance prompted at the audition. "That doesn't bother me because I knew I had to get on with my act ... ," said Boyle, again speaking by satellite. "I wasn't sure how I would be received, so I just thought I'd give it a whirl."  Watch Larry King interview Susan Boyle » . Morgan, too, acknowledged the laughter, including his own. "I sort of feel like apologizing to Susan," he said. "I'm sorry, because we did not give you anything like the respect we should have done when you first came out." He said the judges had been through a long day with "lots of terrible auditions." "And then you came out and we thought you were going to be a bit of a joke act, to be honest with you," he said. "And then I can remember ... that second when you had begun to sing, and I had never heard a more surprising, extraordinary voice coming out of somebody so unexpected." To win the show, which would give her the chance to sing in front of Queen Elizabeth II, Boyle must survive a live semifinal next month and then a final performance if she gets through that.  Watch how things have changed in Boyle's hometown » . "She's the most odds-on favorite ever on 'Britain's Got Talent' at this stage of the competition," Morgan said. "But Susan knows there are two big hurdles left. Anything can happen in a live show." There's already been talk of a recording contract and world tours for Boyle. But she said she's staying focused on the competition for now. She said she has no plans to get a makeover or alter her wardrobe -- "Why should I? Why should I change?" -- but did predict one big lifestyle change. "I won't be lonely," she said. "I certainly won't be lonely anymore."

# Susan Boyle’s Unlikely Rise: From Scottish Village to Global Television Sensation

**LONDON —** In the space of a few minutes on a British talent-show stage, Susan Boyle went from an unknown church volunteer in Scotland to one of the most recognizable voices in the world.

Boyle, then 47, walked onto the set of **“Britain’s Got Talent”** in April 2009 and told judges Simon Cowell, Amanda Holden and Piers Morgan that she dreamed of becoming a professional singer. Her ambition drew skeptical expressions and scattered laughter from an audience apparently judging her by her age, appearance and awkward stage manner.

Then the music began.

Boyle’s powerful rendition of **“I Dreamed a Dream”** from the musical *Les Misérables* transformed the room. Audience members rose to their feet, the judges’ expressions changed from amusement to astonishment, and Boyle received three emphatic “yes” votes.

The audition quickly became an international phenomenon. Video of the performance spread across YouTube, television broadcasts and news websites, attracting tens of millions of views and turning Boyle into an emblem of overlooked talent.

## CNN interviews bring Boyle to an American audience

The attention soon carried Boyle far beyond Britain. CNN featured her in interviews that introduced American viewers to the soft-spoken singer from Blackburn, West Lothian.

Boyle spoke about the speed of her transformation from a private citizen into a worldwide celebrity, describing the experience as exciting but difficult to comprehend. She discussed her years of singing in local venues and church settings, as well as the encouragement she had received from her late mother to pursue a larger stage.

During an appearance connected with CNN’s **“Larry King Live,”** Boyle offered viewers another glimpse of her voice by singing part of **“My Heart Will Go On,”** the Celine Dion hit from *Titanic*. The informal performance reinforced the central appeal of her story: the television audition had not been a one-time trick, and her voice remained striking even without the full theatrical buildup of the talent show.

Her CNN exposure also demonstrated how thoroughly the story had crossed cultural boundaries. “Britain’s Got Talent” was a British program, but Boyle’s audition had become global entertainment news before she had even reached the competition’s later rounds.

## Piers Morgan apologizes for judging her too quickly

Morgan, one of the three judges, became a prominent voice in the coverage. In interviews after the audition, he acknowledged that he had underestimated Boyle before she began singing.

He apologized for prejudging her on the basis of her appearance and demeanor, an admission that captured the larger lesson many viewers took from the performance. Morgan said, in effect, that Boyle had exposed the assumptions of everyone in the room—including the judges.

On the show itself, Morgan had called his vote for Boyle the biggest “yes” he had ever given a contestant. His later apology added another dimension: Boyle’s success was not simply about vocal ability but about the humiliation of those who had dismissed her.

Cowell, known for blunt criticism, was also visibly impressed, while Holden praised Boyle for silencing the audience and forcing viewers to reconsider their first impressions.

## Overnight fame—and intense pressure

Boyle’s rise was often described as overnight, but her musical ambitions had developed over many years. She had performed locally, made amateur recordings and cared for her mother, who had encouraged her to audition for the program. Boyle said she entered “Britain’s Got Talent” partly to honor that encouragement.

Her sudden celebrity brought opportunities, but it also created extraordinary pressure. Reporters gathered in her village, photographers followed her, and every new appearance was analyzed for signs that she could live up to the audition.

That scrutiny raised a crucial question: Could Boyle turn one unforgettable performance into a winning run?

## Could Susan Boyle win “Britain’s Got Talent”?

Immediately after the audition, Boyle became the clear favorite in the eyes of many viewers and British bookmakers. She had several advantages:

- **A distinctive and powerful voice**
- **An emotionally resonant personal story**
- **Enormous international publicity**
- **Strong support from all three judges**
- **A viral performance that viewers wanted to reward**

But winning was not guaranteed. “Britain’s Got Talent” was ultimately decided by the public, and later rounds could change the momentum quickly. Boyle would need to choose songs that suited her voice, manage the expectations created by her first appearance and remain composed under a level of attention she had never previously experienced.

There was also the risk of backlash. Once a contestant becomes an overwhelming favorite, every imperfect note or nervous moment receives greater attention. Rivals—including dance groups, singers and novelty acts—could benefit from being less heavily scrutinized.

Still, at the height of “Susan mania,” the competition appeared to be hers to lose. Her appeal reached beyond the usual talent-show audience, and her audition had become one of the defining television moments of the year.

Boyle ultimately advanced to the 2009 final, where she finished as runner-up to the dance group **Diversity**. Yet the result did little to slow her career. Her debut album, *I Dreamed a Dream*, became an international bestseller, proving that although she did not win the show, she had already won something larger: a global audience.

# Susan Boyle: From lonely village singer to global sensation

**By CNN**  
**April 2009**

**LONDON, England (CNN)** — Less than two weeks ago, Susan Boyle was an unknown church volunteer from a small Scottish village. Today, her soaring voice has been heard by millions around the world.

Boyle, 47, became an overnight sensation after appearing on the British television show “Britain’s Got Talent.” When the unmarried, unemployed singer walked onto the stage and said she dreamed of becoming a professional performer, the judges and audience appeared skeptical.

Then she began singing “I Dreamed a Dream” from the musical “Les Misérables.”

The performance brought the crowd to its feet and left the judges stunned. Video of the audition quickly spread across YouTube and other Web sites, attracting tens of millions of views and turning Boyle into an international celebrity.

Her sudden fame has prompted television appearances, interview requests and speculation that she could win the competition. It has also brought calls for a celebrity-style makeover — something Boyle says she does not need.

“I’m happy the way I am,” she has said, rejecting suggestions that she should dramatically change her hair, clothes or appearance. Boyle has indicated that she wants audiences to focus on her singing rather than her image.

That contrast helped make the audition so memorable. Before Boyle sang, some audience members laughed and rolled their eyes. After the first few notes, their reaction changed instantly.

Judge Simon Cowell called the performance extraordinary, while fellow judge Amanda Holden said Boyle’s audition was a wake-up call for people who had judged her by her appearance.

Boyle comes from Blackburn, a village in West Lothian, Scotland. The youngest of nine children, she cared for her mother until her death and has spoken openly about living a quiet, sometimes isolated life. She has never married and joked during her audition that she had never been kissed.

Now, with fans around the world and a flood of attention, Boyle says her life has changed.

“I won’t be lonely anymore,” she said.

Whether Boyle ultimately wins “Britain’s Got Talent” remains to be seen. But her audition has already become one of the defining moments of the Internet video era — a reminder that talent can emerge from unexpected places and that first impressions can be spectacularly wrong.
